case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Rule 60(b)(4) motion seeking to vacate a default judgment as void for lack of personal jurisdiction is subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s requirement that such motions be brought within a “reasonable time,” or may be brought at any time.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (void judgments) and 60(c)(1) (timing: “within a reasonable time” for motions under Rule 60(b)); underlying due process/personal-jurisdiction principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio, and because void judgments are legal nullities, Rule 60(c)(1) should not impose any time limit on Rule 60(b)(4) motions challenging such judgments. In petitioner’s view, applying a “reasonable time” restriction improperly converts a jurisdictional defect into something like a forfeitable error, allowing a court to leave a void judgment in place merely due to delay.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the text of Rule 60(c)(1) is straightforward: any motion under Rule 60(b)—including (b)(4)—must be filed within a reasonable time. Respondent emphasizes this Court’s recent statement in Kemp that “all” Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time, and contends petitioner’s no-deadline rule would undermine finality and disrupt reliance interests (here, a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate), inviting strategic delay and chaos.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (cited for the proposition that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
Klapprott v. United States, 335 U.S. 601 (1949) (discussed regarding time limits and Rule 60(b)(4) voidness analysis)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010) (cited as suggesting void-judgment attacks may be available and referencing treatises/cases)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990) (cited via Espinosa discussion on void judgments/timing)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970) (comity/registration court discretion reference in the record excerpts)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993) (discretion/comity reference in the record excerpts)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962) (inherent power/docket management reference in the record excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Respondent because Rule 60(c)(1) supplies the threshold limit on a federal court’s authority to reopen a final judgment: it states in mandatory, unqualified terms that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and it contains no carveout for (b)(4). Justice Alito’s sequencing point is decisive—timeliness is the antecedent procedural question, and only if the movant clears that gate do we reach whether the judgment is “void,” a category our precedents treat as narrow rather than a perpetual license to unsettle reliance. Petitioner’s “legal nullity” maxim is strongest in cases of lack of notice, but as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh explain, that concern can be accommodated within the flexible reasonable-time inquiry without rewriting the Rule to create an atextual exemption. Given the near-complete Chapter 7 administration, the reliance and prejudice considerations properly inform what counts as “reasonable,” preserving due process while respecting finality.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention—that a void judgment is a legal nullity susceptible to attack at any time—cannot override the Federal Rules’ text. As the Chief Justice notes, Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and the Rule’s structure confirms the drafters knew how to create categorical timing exceptions when they wished (as with the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3)), yet did not exempt (b)(4). Justice Alito is right about sequencing: timeliness under (c)(1) is a threshold condition on the court’s authority to reopen, and only then do we reach whether the judgment is void. On these facts, where a Chapter 7 estate has been substantially administered and reliance interests have crystallized, “reasonable time” has real force and bars a belated Rule 60(b)(4) motion without inventing an atextual carveout.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s “legal nullity” maxim is the best they have, but it cannot do the work of rewriting Rule 60(c)(1), which by its terms governs any motion “under Rule 60(b)” and contains no carveout for (b)(4). I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas that we must address first the threshold question whether the court has rule-based power to reopen a final judgment—timeliness—before reaching the downstream contention that the original judgment was void for lack of personal jurisdiction. The reasonable-time standard is sufficiently flexible to account for genuine lack-of-notice situations without converting (b)(4) into a perpetual reopening device, and the reliance interests emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh are especially weighty given the near-complete administration of the Chapter 7 estate. Nothing in the colleagues’ discussion supplies a doctrinally grounded distinction that would justify creating an atextual exemption here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument remains the maxim that a void judgment is a legal nullity subject to attack at any time, but that principle cannot displace Rule 60’s own sequencing and limits on collateral reopening. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b)” and contains no carveout for (b)(4); creating a timeless exception would invite serial, destabilizing collateral attacks precisely when finality and reliance interests are at their apex, as in this nearly administered Chapter 7 estate. The better way to respect truly void judgments is through the flexible “reasonable time” inquiry—which can account for lack of notice or inability to act—without rewriting the Rule into an unlimited reopening mechanism. On these facts, the reliance and delay concerns make the district court’s timeliness determination a proper threshold barrier before reaching the merits of “voidness,” as Justice Alito notes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains the traditional maxim that a void judgment is a legal nullity, and so can be attacked at any time—but that principle cannot override the Federal Rules’ timing architecture. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b)” and contains no carveout for (b)(4); after Kemp, we should be especially wary of implying an exemption the text does not supply. Functionally, making (b)(4) timeless would convert Rule 60 from a bounded, post-judgment corrective mechanism into a perpetual reopening device, undermining finality and reliance interests that are acute here given the near-complete Chapter 7 administration. The right way to respect truly jurisdictionless or notice-deficient cases is within the flexible ‘reasonable time’ inquiry—not by reading an atextual no-deadline rule into the Rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains the traditional maxim that a void judgment is a nullity and so may be attacked at any time, but we are not writing on a blank slate—we are applying Rule 60 as written. As the Chief Justice notes, Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that a motion “under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and it supplies no textual carveout for (b)(4); the Rule’s structure (one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3)) confirms the drafters knew how to create distinct timing regimes when they wished. Justice Kavanaugh’s emphasis on the fact-dependent nature of “reasonable time” answers the due-process concern without converting (b)(4) into a perpetual reopening device, especially where reliance interests are acute in a nearly administered Chapter 7 estate. We should treat timeliness as the threshold inquiry, and only if the movant clears it do we reach whether the judgment is truly “void” in the narrow sense our precedents recognize.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument is the longstanding maxim that a truly void judgment is a legal nullity and thus open to attack at any time. But as the Chief Justice explains, our authority to reopen final judgments in federal court here runs through Rule 60, and Rule 60(c)(1) states in mandatory terms that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” with no textual carveout for (b)(4)—a point reinforced by Justice Kagan’s reliance on Kemp’s instruction that the reasonable-time requirement applies to all Rule 60(b) motions. The reasonable-time standard is also administrable and accommodates the exceptional case (e.g., lack of notice) without creating a perpetual reopening regime that would undermine finality and third-party reliance interests, particularly acute in a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate as Justice Barrett emphasized. Any categorical “timeless” exception for (b)(4) is better viewed as a policy innovation for the rulemaking process, not something we should judicially add to the Rule’s structure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s “legal nullity” maxim has intuitive force in the personal-jurisdiction context, but it cannot supply an atextual exemption from Rule 60(c)(1)’s categorical command that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the Rule’s structure confirms the point: the drafters knew how to impose different timing rules and did so expressly for (b)(1)–(3), leaving (b)(4) within the reasonable-time baseline rather than outside all temporal limits. Justice Alito is right that timeliness is the threshold question of the court’s rule-based authority to reopen a final judgment; only if that condition is satisfied do we reach whether the judgment is void. And as Justice Kagan notes, reading (b)(4) as timeless would produce an administratively perverse, reliance-disrupting regime—especially in a nearly administered Chapter 7 estate—without textual warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point—the maxim that a void judgment is a legal nullity subject to attack at any time—cannot supersede the Federal Rules’ own framework for post-judgment reopening. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) imposes a Rule-wide, mandatory “reasonable time” limit on any motion “under Rule 60(b),” with no textual carveout for (b)(4); treating (b)(4) as timeless would collapse the Rule’s finality-justice balance and effectively create an atextual exception. Consistent with the mutual exclusivity of Rule 60(b)’s subsections, this motion belongs under (b)(4), but that categorization selects the ground for relief—it does not displace the threshold timeliness requirement. On abuse-of-discretion review, it was permissible for the district court to conclude that an unexplained delay, coupled with substantial reliance interests in a nearly administered Chapter 7 estate, rendered the motion untimely even assuming voidness is narrowly defined.

John Roberts.reasoning: The starting point is the Rules’ own framework: Rule 60(c)(1) states that a motion under Rule 60(b)—without excluding subsection (b)(4)—must be made “within a reasonable time,” and reading (b)(4) as exempt would require an atextual carveout inconsistent with the Rule’s structure. Our void-judgment cases also treat “void” in Rule 60(b)(4) as a narrow category (reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable jurisdictional basis), and they make clear that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to sleep on one’s rights when the movant had notice and an opportunity to object. On these facts, where the judgment has long since been relied upon in a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate, allowing an anytime attack would disserve finality and fairness, and the “reasonable time” inquiry can accommodate genuine lack-of-notice situations without converting due-process limits into forfeitable merits errors. Because the case can be resolved on the Rules’ text and our conduct-and-fairness understanding of due process and voidness, there is no need to adopt broader theories that would unsettle settled judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in the text, structure, or history of Rule 60 carves out an exception for motions brought under Rule 60(b)(4). The Rule’s architecture reinforces that conclusion: the drafters imposed an additional one-year cap for reasons (1)–(3) but chose not to create a different timing rule for (b)(4), so we should not rewrite the Rule to add a no-deadline regime. Treating (b)(4) motions as exempt would dilute Rule 60(c)(1)’s command by importing an atextual “legal nullity” concept that displaces the Rule’s sequencing—first satisfy the invoked subsection, but still comply with the timing framework the Rule expressly attaches to all 60(b) motions. On these facts—where the movant waited long enough that the opposing side asserts substantial reliance/finality interests in a nearly administered Chapter 7 estate—the “reasonable time” requirement has real work to do, and the motion may be denied as untimely without converting personal-jurisdiction limits into a forfeitable merits error.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The threshold question is the court’s procedural authority to reopen a final judgment under the Federal Rules, and Rule 60(c)(1) states in mandatory terms that a motion “under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” without carving out an exception for (b)(4). Treating petitioner’s filing by its substance, it is a Rule 60(b)(4) request to reopen the default judgment; that procedural power exists only on the conditions the Rule itself imposes, and the Rule’s structure (including a special one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3) but none for (b)(4)) confirms that (b)(4) remains governed by the “reasonable time” requirement rather than exempt from timing limits altogether. Allowing an at-any-time attack would expand what the Rules accomplish beyond their proper role and would undermine finality and reliance interests in the specific posture here, where the judgment has been relied on in the near-complete administration of a Chapter 7 estate. Once timeliness (the court’s authority to reopen) is resolved under Rule 60(c)(1), only then may a court proceed to the downstream question whether the judgment is actually void for lack of personal jurisdiction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(b)(4) functions as a collateral attack on a completed judgment and, under settled doctrine, a Rule 60(b) motion “does not affect the [original] judgment’s finality or suspend its operation,” instead proceeding as a separate, later challenge—precisely the posture in which timing limits serve finality and delay-prevention values. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) to exempt (b)(4) motions would invite serial, strategic delay and destabilize reliance interests built on the judgment’s continued operation (here, a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate), undermining the systemic interest in finality that the Rules are designed to protect. The text of Rule 60(c)(1) draws no (b)(4) exception, and this Court’s recent instruction that “all” Rule 60(b) motions must be filed “within a reasonable time” confirms that the proper balance is enforced through the reasonable-time inquiry rather than an unlimited collateral-attack regime. On these facts—where the judgment has long operated and third-party reliance has accrued—the reasonable-time requirement is essential to prevent exactly the kind of disruptive after-the-fact undoing petitioner seeks.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Rules’ text and structure resolve the timing question: Rule 60(c)(1) says that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in that provision carves out Rule 60(b)(4). Reading (b)(4) as exempt would disrupt the procedural architecture that ties post-judgment mechanisms to finality and reliance, especially where (as here) the default judgment has been treated as operative long enough to shape substantial downstream reliance (a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate). Consistent with how courts have long treated Rule 60 as a limited, administrable avenue for relief rather than a perpetual reopen-the-case device, “voidness” under (b)(4) can justify strong merits relief in exceptional jurisdictional-defect cases, but it does not erase Rule 60(c)(1)’s independent, rule-based timing constraint. On these facts, allowing an at-any-time attack would invite strategic delay and undermine the system of settled judgments the Rules are designed to protect.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) says that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in the text or structure carves out an exception for motions under Rule 60(b)(4); indeed, the Rule’s choice to impose an extra one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3) underscores that other subsections—including (b)(4)—remain governed by the reasonable-time requirement. Treating (b)(4) as timeless would rewrite the Rule and tilt the finality/error-correction balance in a policy-laden way better left to ordinary appellate channels or the Rules Enabling Act process, especially where (as here) parties and third parties have proceeded in reliance on a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate. And because “reasonable time” is a fact-dependent inquiry, it is entirely appropriate to consider delay and reliance interests in deciding whether this particular motion—brought long after default—comes too late even if the movant now alleges a personal-jurisdiction defect. Kemp’s instruction that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1) supplies the controlling textual anchor for that conclusion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The starting point is the text and the default procedural rule: Rule 60(c)(1) states that a motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a “reasonable time,” and nothing in the Rule clearly carves out an exception for (b)(4) void-judgment motions. This Court’s decision in Kemp recently underscored that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to that reasonable-time requirement, and absent a clear contrary directive in the Rules or controlling precedent, the baseline timing rule controls. Applying a reasonable-time standard is also more administrable and fair in practice because it protects finality and reliance interests—particularly where, as here, a default judgment has been relied on to administer a Chapter 7 estate—while still leaving room for courts to treat truly void, jurisdictionally defective judgments differently in determining what is “reasonable.” Petitioner’s no-deadline rule would invite strategic delay and undermine orderly administration, and any categorical change is better addressed through the rulemaking process rather than judicially creating an extra-textual exception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with the text and structure: Rule 60(c)(1) states that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and it then adds a separate one-year cap only for reasons (1), (2), and (3)—a structure that shows the drafters knew how to create differentiated timing rules and did not exempt (b)(4). Reading an atextual carveout into (c)(1) would override what the Rule “demands” and invite an administratively unworkable regime in which default judgments could be attacked decades later, notwithstanding reliance interests—here, a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate. That does not convert personal-jurisdiction limits into mere forfeitable error: it recognizes that Rule 60 supplies a procedural vehicle, and the Rules themselves contemplate timeliness constraints even when the asserted defect is jurisdictional. The reasonable-time inquiry also avoids an “empty exercise” by permitting prompt correction of genuinely void judgments while preventing strategic delay that would undermine finality without any textual warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(b) provides a limited, post-judgment reopening mechanism that must be applied according to its structure, and Rule 60(c)(1) states in categorical terms that motions under Rule 60(b) must be made "within a reasonable time"—with only (b)(1)–(3) subject to an additional one-year cap. Because Rule 60(b)’s subsections are mutually exclusive, this case is properly analyzed under 60(b)(4), but that categorization does not exempt the movant from Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement; instead, it means the motion is governed by “reasonable time,” not the one-year limit. Applying Rule 60(b)’s core finality/justice balance to these facts—where the judgment is long final and the respondent and third parties have relied (including a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate)—a no-deadline rule would invite strategic delay and destabilize reliance interests in a way inconsistent with Rule 60(b)’s disciplined, limited role. On abuse-of-discretion review, a district court acts consistently with Rule 60(b)’s core tenets when it treats substantial, unexplained delay as rendering a 60(b)(4) request untimely in light of prejudice and settled expectations, while still leaving room for prompt challenges to truly void judgments.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a motion under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) to vacate a default judgment that is void for lack of personal jurisdiction can be denied as untimely under Rule 60(c)(1)’s requirement that Rule 60(b) motions be made within a “reasonable time.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (relief from a judgment that “is void”) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) (a “motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio and therefore a Rule 60(b)(4) motion to vacate such a judgment should not be subject to any time limit—including Rule 60(c)(1)’s “reasonable time” requirement—because a void judgment is a legal nullity that may be attacked at any time.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the text of Rule 60(c)(1) unambiguously applies to all Rule 60(b) motions, including 60(b)(4), so a party cannot wait an unreasonable length of time to challenge a judgment as void; the Sixth Circuit’s application of a reasonable-time limit is consistent with Supreme Court guidance and is necessary to protect finality and prevent disruption (including to a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 bankruptcy estate).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s function-over-caption point is the most serious obstacle: if the motion was filed within Rule 59(e)’s non-extendable 28-day window and truly “questions the correctness” of the judgment, longstanding practice would treat it as Rule 59(e) for Rule 4(a)(4) purposes. But that principle presupposes the predicate fact—timeliness under Rule 59(e)—and it does not answer Justice Thomas’s structural concern that courts must first identify the proper Rule 60(b) subsection (and enforce its anti-circumvention limits) when the movant invokes Rule 60 and seeks relief that in substance fits (b)(1)–(3). Justice Sotomayor’s finality emphasis reinforces, rather than undermines, the need for a rule-bound characterization before we let the label alter appeal timing. The most institutionally sound course remains a narrow disposition clarifying the governing characterization framework and remanding for application on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s function-over-caption point has force where the filing is, in substance and timing, a Rule 59(e) motion, but it cannot do the work respondents need if the movant affirmatively invoked Rule 60(b) grounds that fit within (b)(1)–(3) and thus trigger Rule 60(c)(1)’s one-year cap and “reasonable time” policing against end-runs. Justice Barrett’s observation that recharacterizing into Rule 59(e) can be “stricter” does not answer the antecedent structural question: Rule 60(b)(6) is unavailable when another subsection applies, and courts should not convert a Rule 60 motion into Rule 59(e) to alter downstream finality and appeal consequences without first respecting that channeling. As Justice Alito and the Chief Justice emphasized, the proper method is to classify the motion under the Rules’ text and structure and then apply the corresponding standards; importing a generalized functional test risks diluting Rule 60(b)’s subsection-specific constraints and inviting the very manipulation Rule 60(c)(1) is designed to deter. Absent a record feature showing this was actually a timely, merits-directed reconsideration motion rather than a Rule 60 collateral attack, I remain with Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett press the entrenched function-over-caption practice for timely merits-reconsideration motions, but that approach still presupposes an antecedent, rule-text characterization of what procedural vehicle the movant actually invoked and what relief it substantively seeks. If the motion in substance asks to set aside a final judgment on grounds cognizable under Rule 60(b)—and especially if it maps onto (b)(1)–(3)—we cannot bypass Rule 60’s subsection channeling and time limits simply by invoking a functional appeal-clock doctrine, as Justice Thomas underscores. Justice Sotomayor is right that Rule 59(e)’s fixed 28-day window is the system’s anti-manipulation line; but that cuts against recharacterization that would alter downstream jurisdictional or finality consequences without first resolving whether Rule 60(b) is being used to relitigate the merits rather than to correct a defect in the prior proceeding. And, as the Kokkonen/Badgerow principle reminds, Rule 60(b) can reopen only within the court’s existing jurisdictional bounds—it cannot be treated as a free-floating equitable power to reorder finality when the predicate procedural authorization is uncertain on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s function-over-caption principle has force only for motions filed within Rule 59(e)’s fixed, non-extendable 28-day window; once that window closes, the Rules deliberately channel litigants to Rule 60(b), with different consequences for finality and appellate timing. The Petitioners’ strongest point, pressed by Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh, is that courts must police Rule 60(b)’s subsection limits and not permit strategic relabeling to evade the one-year bar and other structural constraints—but that concern supports, rather than undermines, a bright line at Rule 59(e)’s deadline: untimely merits reconsideration cannot be treated as Rule 59(e) to toll the appeal clock. Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed remand for a characterization framework is appealing institutionally, yet absent a concrete, case-specific feature showing this filing was actually timely (or otherwise fits Rule 59(e)’s prompt self-correction function), I would adhere to the Rules’ timing architecture and the anti-delay/finality principles reflected in Stone v. INS. On this record, treating an out-of-time reconsideration motion as Rule 59(e) would invite manipulation of Appellate Rule 4(a)(4) and erode the finality structure the Rules are designed to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Rule 60(b) has subsection-specific constraints, and courts must not let (b)(6) become an end-run around the one-year bar for (b)(1)–(3). But that concern assumes we are properly in Rule 60(b) at all; the characterization question comes first, and entrenched appellate practice treats a timely post-judgment motion that “questions the correctness” of the judgment as Rule 59(e) regardless of caption, precisely because it bears on finality and the appeal clock. Justice Barrett is right that this recharacterization runs into Rule 59(e)’s stricter, nonextendable 28-day limit—so it does not evade Rule 60’s structure but instead enforces the integrated scheme reflected in Appellate Rule 4(a)(4). Chief Justice Roberts’s suggestion of a narrow remand has appeal, but without a case-specific feature showing this motion is outside the prototypical timely merits-reconsideration filing, I would not adopt a rigid label-bound approach that departs from how lower courts have long administered these rules.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett press the best respondent-side point: when a postjudgment motion is filed within Rule 59(e)’s 28-day window and functionally “questions the correctness” of the judgment, longstanding practice may treat it as Rule 59(e) for Appellate Rule 4(a)(4) purposes. But that functional approach cannot do the work they assign it unless the motion is in fact timely under—and substantively of the kind contemplated by—Rule 59(e); otherwise the Rules deliberately channel litigants into Rule 60(b), with its subsection-specific gates and Rule 60(c)(1)’s distinct timeliness command. As Justice Thomas and the Chief Justice emphasize, we should not collapse those lines by adopting a transsubstantive recharacterization rule that risks converting Rule 60 into an end-run around the remedial scheme (Rule 59(e), appeal, then limited collateral relief), especially when “reasonable time” under Rule 60(c)(1) is meant to remain a case-by-case inquiry rather than a fixed surrogate deadline. If the record is uncertain on these predicates, the sounder course is a narrow disposition identifying the proper characterization framework and remanding for application, rather than announcing a categorical rule better suited to the Rules Enabling Act process.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the entrenched “function over caption” practice for timely reconsideration motions, and Justice Barrett adds that recharacterizing into Rule 59(e) runs toward (not away from) a stricter deadline. But that functional practice cannot be applied in a way that collapses the Rules’ deliberate structural distinctions: as Justice Thomas emphasizes, Rule 60(b) relief is subsection-gated with specific time constraints, and courts should not use relabeling to bypass those limits or to alter finality consequences without first determining the proper procedural vehicle under the text. Chief Justice Roberts’ administrability concern reinforces that appellate-jurisdiction timing rules need a predictable, rules-based characterization framework rather than an after-the-fact equitable relabeling approach. On this record, I do not see a respondent-side precedent or tradition compelling a broader recharacterization rule than our cabined framework, so I remain with Petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest petitioner-side point, pressed by Justice Thomas and echoed by the Chief Justice, is that Rule 60(b)’s subsection-specific limits cannot be evaded by relabeling, and that we should not manipulate captions to destabilize finality and appellate jurisdiction. But Justice Kagan’s function-over-caption principle is itself a rule-bound, text-and-structure account of the integrated scheme: a motion filed within Rule 59(e)’s non-extendable 28-day window that challenges the judgment’s correctness is treated as Rule 59(e) for FRAP 4(a)(4)(A) purposes, and that moves in the direction of stricter timing rather than circumvention. Justice Sotomayor is right that finality cuts against extending Rule 59(e) beyond 28 days; yet precisely because the 28-day line is fixed, characterizing timely merits-reconsideration motions as Rule 59(e) better preserves the Rules’ design than locking parties into an erroneous Rule 60 label. If the record is unclear on timeliness or the motion’s functional content, a narrow remand may be appropriate, but the governing characterization principle should be the Rule 59(e) functional inquiry rather than starting from Rule 60.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s structural warning that Rule 60(b)(6) cannot become an end-run around the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3) is a serious rule-of-law concern, and I agree courts must police subsection channeling once Rule 60(b) is truly in play. But Justice Kagan (and now Justice Barrett) persuasively identify an antecedent, practice-rooted point: when a postjudgment motion is filed within Rule 59(e)’s fixed window and functionally challenges the correctness of the judgment, courts routinely treat it as Rule 59(e) for finality and Appellate Rule 4(a)(4) purposes—so the anti-circumvention logic cuts in favor of recharacterizing into the stricter regime, not away from it. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow remand underscores how fact- and function-dependent this inquiry is; on this record, I’m not prepared to adopt a rigid label-driven approach that risks forfeiting review for timely litigants based on captioning rather than substance. Unless the petitioner can point to case-specific indicia of manipulation or a basis to conclude this filing is substantively a late Rule 60(b) collateral attack, procedural fairness and the integrated Rules scheme keep me with the Respondent.
